description: We are a team of Japanese students. Global participants are welcome! Let's discuss things and get to know each other!
summary:
Mission Return is a cooperative game for 1–4 players, inspired by Apollo 13, that takes a crew from spacecraft design to splashdown in about 7 minutes. Players first design their mission: choosing parts within mass and budget limits, then selecting an orbit and a rocket. After launch, an oxygen tank fails on the way to the Moon. From that moment, power, oxygen, temperature, and CO₂ change every second, and the crew must work together across separate seats, flipping switches, pointing the spacecraft, collecting science data behind the Moon, and choosing a return route before the burn window closes.

There is no branching script. Every outcome comes from one live simulation, so the choices made in design decide what is possible in the emergency, and return trajectories are computed with NASA’s GMAT. The game shows why real missions depend on trade-offs, margins, and teamwork and lets anyone experience them firsthand.
details:
Mission Return

What is this game?

Mission Return is a cooperative game for 1–4 players that takes a crew from spacecraft design to splashdown in about 7 minutes. This game was inspired by the Apollo 13 incident.

  1. Pilot: Spacecraft attitude, course correction, ignition
  2. Life Support: Oxygen valves, CO₂ filter
  3. Comms & Power: Heater, lights, navigation, comms, data transmission
  4. Mission Planner: Science instruments, return route; the only seat that sees the orbit map and the countdowns

Benefits

Players learn mission design by living with their own decisions, not by reading about them.

  • Every part costs mass, money, and power, so players have to give something up. A science instrument that looked cheap on the design screen can drain the battery later, when the crew needs the heater.
  • Spare batteries and oxygen tanks feel like wasted mass until the accident. After that, they often decide which ending you get.
  • Players have to talk to each other. Only the mission planner can see the orbit map and the countdowns, and some actions only work if two players press at the same moment.
  • One session takes about 7 minutes and runs in a browser, so it is easy to use in a class or at an event.
  • The return trajectories were computed with NASA's GMAT, and the timeline follows the Apollo 13 mission report.

Intended impact

We want the audience to get a feel for why space missions are designed the way they are. In one sitting, students or visitors at an outreach event can go through a whole mission, from the requirements to the post-flight review.

After splashdown, the report shows which of the four requirements the crew met and what they did. We hope players see that a safe return depends on the design as much as on the flying and then try again with a different spacecraft.


Tools, languages, and software

The game is a Unity client that draws the spacecraft and sends button presses, and a Python server that owns the simulation and ticks once per second for all players.

  1. Game client. Unity 6 (URP), C#. Builds for the browser (WebGL).
  2. Simulation server. Python, FastAPI, and WebSockets, hosted on Vercel.
  3. Game balance. 77 parameters and a parts catalog kept in JSON, generated from a spreadsheet, so balance changes need no code changes
  4. Orbits. NASA GMAT R2026a. Our own script computes return routes A and B; the CSV output draws the orbit map
  5. 3D models. Blender.
  6. Voice and sound. Houston's lines written by the team and read by Google Gemini TTS; sound effects synthesized in Python; music and UI sounds from CC0 and Pixabay libraries
  7. Development. Git and GitHub, Claude Code as a coding assistant.

NASA data and documents in the game:

  • GMAT trajectories. A free-return orbit passing 254 km above the far side of the Moon, with a fast return (0.271 km/s burn, 63.0 hours to reentry) and a slow return (0.052 km/s, 70.6 hours).
  • Apollo 13 audio. The real "Houston, we've had a problem" transmission plays at the moment of the accident.
  • Imagery. Earth from Blue Marble: Next Generation and the Moon from the CGI Moon Kit.
  • Documents. The Apollo 13 Mission Report, the Review Board report and the Apollo Flight Journal set the order and timing of events.
  • NASA 3D Resources. The Apollo spacecraft models were used to measure proportions; our models were rebuilt from those measurements.

Play it.

The game is built for young students with no aerospace background: each friend takes one seat, and the trade-offs teach themselves.
